summary: חָנָה is to stop and pitch camp: Israel in the wilderness “set out” (נָסַע) and “encamped” (חָנָה) at Yahweh’s command as the cloud moved or rested (Num 9:17–23; Num 33), an army encamps against a city to besiege it (1Sa 11:1; Jer 52:4), and the angel of Yahweh encamps around those who fear him (Psa 34:8). Once it is the day “declining” toward evening (Jdg 19:9), the sense the Arabic and Syriac ḥny “bend” share; how “bend” and “encamp” join is not shown by the text. מַחֲנֶה is the camp, the company encamped, and so an army, Israel’s camp being holy because Yahweh walked in its midst (Deu 23:15), so that the unclean and the sin offering were put outside it (Lev 16:27), where Christ suffered (Heb 13:11–13). The spear חֲנִית and the vaulted cell חָנוּת are filed here too, the spear’s tie to the root unclear.

senses.definition: The place where a people on the move has pitched its tents, with an inside, a gate and an outside: Israel’s camp in the wilderness, laid out by standards around the tent of meeting, which set out at the trumpets’ call.

evidence.note: The tent of meeting sets out, the camp of the Levites in the midst of the camps (הַמַּחֲנֹת): as they encamp, so they set out.
The two silver trumpets are for calling the congregation and for the journeying of the camps.
At the alarm the camps lying east set out.
The standard of the camp of the sons of Judah set out first.
The cloud of Yahweh was over them by day when they set out from the camp.
Moses stands in the gate of the camp.
Eldad and Medad stay in the camp and prophesy there, not going out to the tent.
Moses pitches the tent outside the camp, far from the camp, and all who seek Yahweh go out to it.
The unclean man dwells alone; outside the camp is his dwelling.
The bull and goat of the sin offering are carried outside the camp and burned.
The unclean are sent outside the camp, that they defile not their camps in whose midst Yahweh dwells.
Yahweh walks in the midst of your camp, so your camp shall be holy.
Miriam is shut outside the camp seven days.
The generation of men of war perished from the midst of the camp.
The bodies of the beasts whose blood is brought into the holy place are burned outside the camp (παρεμβολή), as Lev 16:27.

senses.definition: The people, with their flocks and goods, who travel and encamp together: a company, not only the place where it lies.

evidence.note: Jacob divides the people with him, and the flocks, herds and camels, into two camps.
Esau asks, “What do you mean by all this camp which I met?”
Chariots and horsemen go up with Joseph to bury Jacob, and the camp is very great.
The quails fall in the midst of Israel’s camp, round about their dwellings.

senses.definition: An army in the field, named as the camp it forms; also Yahweh’s own host, his angels or the forces he sends.

evidence.note: The cloud comes between the camp of Egypt and the camp of Israel, and the one came not near the other all night.
The barley loaf tumbles into the camp of Midian and overturns the tent.
David will give the carcases of the camp of the Philistines to the birds.
The angel of Yahweh strikes in the camp of Assyria 185,000 men.
Joshua hears “a noise of war in the camp”.
“Though a camp encamp against me, my heart shall not fear”, beside war rising against him.
Meeting God’s angels, Jacob says, “This is the camp of God,” and names the place מַחֲנָיִם, “two camps”.
Men came to David day by day, until it was a great camp, like the camp of God.
Yahweh utters his voice before his army (חֵילוֹ), for his camp is very great.
The sound of the living creatures’ wings is like the noise of a camp.
“As the dance of the two camps (הַמַּחֲנָיִם)”.
By faith they turned to flight the camps (παρεμβολάς) of the foreigners.

greek.gloss: camp; army in battle array; barracks

evidence.locator: מַחֲנֶה → παρεμβολή ×126 (lemma count, MACULA alignment), with other cases of the same word; Lev.16.27, מִחוּץ לַמַּחֲנֶה → ἔξω τῆς παρεμβολῆς

evidence.note: The sin offering burned outside the camp (Lev 16:27).
“Let us go forth therefore to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach.”
They compassed the camp of the saints and the beloved city.
Paul is led into the castle (the Roman soldiers’ quarters).

parallels.note: Yahweh’s army set beside his camp.
A camp encamping against him beside war rising against him.

phrases.gloss: outside the camp: where the unclean dwelt, the sin offering was burned and the condemned were stoned
the camp of God, his host

stems.gloss: decline (of the day); encamp, pitch camp; encamp against, besiege; encamp around, guard

senses.definition: Of the day, to sink toward its end: the only use of the verb not about camping.

evidence.note: “The day has sunk (רָפָה) toward evening… behold, the declining of the day (חֲנוֹת הַיּוֹם); lodge here.”

senses.definition: To stop on a journey and set up camp, the opposite of setting out (נָסַע): Israel at each station of the wilderness, and anyone halting to lodge or settle.

evidence.note: When the cloud was taken up they set out, and in the place where the cloud dwelt (יִשְׁכָּן) there they encamped.
“At the mouth of Yahweh they set out, and at the mouth of Yahweh they encamped.”
“They set out from Rameses and encamped in Succoth”: the pattern of the whole itinerary (Num 33:5–49).
Every man by his own standard, they shall encamp round about the tent of meeting.
The camps that encamp (הַחֹנִים) eastward set out at the alarm.
Moses to Hobab: “You know our encamping in the wilderness, and you will be to us for eyes.”
Yahweh went before them to search out a place for them to encamp.
Israel encamped there before the mountain.
Isaac encamped in the valley of Gerar and dwelt there.
Jacob encamped before the city of Shechem.
Ezra’s company encamped three days by the river Ahava.
Those who had killed or touched the slain encamp outside the camp seven days.
Joab and the servants of the king are encamped in the open field.
Armies encamp facing each other.
Judah encamped (settled) from Beersheba to the valley of Hinnom.

senses.definition: With עַל, to pitch camp against a city or a man to attack or besiege him.

evidence.note: Nahash encamped against Jabesh Gilead, and its men offered to serve him.
Nebuchadnezzar and all his army encamped against Jerusalem and built siegeworks round about it.
“Encamp against the city and take it.”
Abimelech encamped at Thebez and took it.
Midian encamped against Israel and destroyed the produce of the land.
Yahweh to Ariel: “I will encamp against you round about, and besiege you with a mound.”
“Though a camp encamp against me.”
God’s troops raise up their way against Job and encamp around his tent.
God scattered the bones of him who encamps against you.

senses.definition: To camp around someone or something as its guard: the Levites around the dwelling, Yahweh’s angel around those who fear him, Yahweh around his house.

evidence.note: The Levites encamp round about the dwelling of the testimony, so that there be no wrath on the congregation, and keep its charge.
Moses, Aaron and his sons encamp before the dwelling eastward, keeping the charge of the sanctuary; the stranger who comes near is put to death.
“The angel of Yahweh encamps round about those who fear him, and delivers them.”
“I will encamp about my house as a guard… and no oppressor shall pass through them any more.”
Saul lay within the ring of the camp and the people encamped around him.

evidence.locator: חָנָה → παρενέβαλον, παρενέβαλεν, παρεμβαλοῦσιν and other forms of παρεμβάλλω (the alignment files most of them under περιβάλλω, a lemma error); Num.9.18, יַחֲנוּ → παρεμβαλοῦσιν. The New Testament as the Textus Receptus reads it does not use the verb.

opposites.note: Setting out against encamping: the two verbs of every station of the wilderness journey.

parallels.note: Where the cloud dwelt, there Israel encamped; as long as it dwelt on the dwelling, they stayed encamped.

phrases.gloss: at the mouth (command) of Yahweh they encamped

words.summary: The spear, thrust or hurled, Saul’s constant weapon. It is filed under this root, but no verse or cognate ties it to “bend” or “encamp”; Egyptian borrowed the same word, ḥnyt “spear”, from a Semitic language, which shows the word with ḥ, but not its link to the root.

senses.definition: A long weapon with a wooden shaft and an iron head, thrust or hurled; named with the sword, the shield and the javelin.

evidence.note: The shaft (עֵץ) of Goliath’s spear was like a weaver’s beam, and its blade (לַהֶבֶת) weighed six hundred shekels of iron.
“You come to me with a sword, and with a spear, and with a javelin; but I come to you in the name of Yahweh of hosts.”
Saul hurled the spear, thinking to pin David to the wall.
Saul struck the spear into the wall.
Abner struck Asahel with the butt of the spear, and the spear came out behind him.
The Philistines allowed no smith in Israel, lest the Hebrews make sword or spear.
The flashing spear and javelin rattle against the war horse.
Abishai lifted up his spear against three hundred slain.

senses.definition: Saul’s spear, kept by him sitting, sleeping and judging, as the mark of the king.

evidence.note: Saul sat under the tamarisk in Gibeah, his spear in his hand, his servants standing about him.
Saul lay asleep, his spear stuck in the ground at his head.
David takes the spear at his head rather than lift his hand against Yahweh’s anointed.
“Behold the king’s spear!”
Jehoiada gives the captains King David’s spear and shields from the house of Yahweh.

senses.definition: The spear as a figure of war ended, of Yahweh’s weapon for his people, and of cruel speech.

evidence.note: They shall beat their swords into ploughshares and their spears into pruning hooks; nation shall not learn war any more.
He makes wars cease to the end of the earth; he breaks the bow and cuts the spear in pieces.
“Draw out the spear, and close the way against my pursuers.”
Sun and moon stood still at the gleam of your glittering spear.
Men whose teeth are spear and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword.

words.summary: Once only, of the cells of the cistern-house where Jeremiah was held. Aramaic and Syriac ḥānūṯā is a chamber, booth or shop, and Arabic ḥaniyya, from the verb “bend”, is a bowed structure, so the cell is probably named from its vaulted roof; the one verse does not show the shape.

senses.definition: A chamber of the cistern-house where a prisoner was kept.

evidence.note: Jeremiah came into the house of the pit and into the cells (הַחֲנֻיוֹת), and remained there many days.

words.summary: Once only, the king of Aram’s word for where he will camp.

senses.definition: The place where an army pitches its camp, or its camping there.

evidence.note: The king of Aram took counsel: “In such and such a place shall be my camp (תַּחֲנֹתִי).”

words.summary: The Peshitta’s word for the “taverns” (Latin tabernae) of the place called Three Taverns, on the road to Rome: a booth or shop, the Syriac answer to Hebrew חָנוּת.

senses.definition: A booth or shop where travellers were served, in the name of a halting place.

evidence.note: The brethren from Rome come to meet Paul as far as Appii Forum and Three Taverns, Syriac ܬܠܬ ܚܢܘܢ, the plural of this word for the Greek Τριῶν Ταβερνῶν.

cognates.gloss: bend, curve; be bent, bow oneself
cognates.note: Lane’s sources give حَنَاهُ “he bent it, curved it”, of a branch or one’s back; حَنَاهُ الدَّهْرُ “time bent him” with age; انحنى “it became bent”, of a man bowed by age; and a curve or bend of a valley or of ground. The day “declining” in Jdg 19:9 is the same bending down. Arabic ḥ (ح), not ḫ (خ), stands behind ח. Lane also gives the root as “act affectionately” of a mother caring for her children; that has no counterpart in this Hebrew root.

evidence.locator: p. 660, root حنو, حَنَاهُ (n9363); انحنى (n9364); p. 661, مَحْنِيَةٌ (n9383)

cognates.gloss: a bow; a bowed or vaulted structure
cognates.note: A bow, “so called because it is bent”, and a bowed, or curved, structure or building: a vaulted building named from the verb “bend”, as חָנוּת may be. Lane also gives حَانُوت “shop, wine-shop”, which some of his sources derive from this root, likened to the حَنِيَّة, and others treat as of another measure; it is probably the Aramaic ḥānūṯā borrowed, and is not counted here.
SEDRA files the verb “bend” and the noun ܚܢܘܬܐ “tavern, store” under one root ḥnʾ, as Hebrew files חָנָה and חָנוּת together. The verb is not used in the Peshitta New Testament.

evidence.locator: root ḥnʾ (root 652), lexeme ܚܢܐ “bend” (1087), lexeme ܚܢܘܬܐ “tavern, store” (1088)

cognates.note: Jewish Aramaic “shop”; the Targum renders the cells of Jer 37:16 by its plural חֶנְוָתָא, keeping the same word. Syriac ܚܢܘܬܐ “tavern, store” is the same noun.

evidence.locator: חֲנוּתָא (H01272): Targ. Jer. XXXVII, 16, pl. חֶנְוָתָא

cognates.note: Phoenician and Punic mḥnt is the army: “any king or governor or commander of the army” (KAI 1.2), “army upon army” (KAI 26 A I 6–8), “a member of the army”, a soldier (CIS i 5866), and in Latin-era inscriptions the consul, “head of the army”. It is the noun מַחֲנֶה in its sense “army”; the same dictionary lists a verb ḥny “make camp”, known only from these nouns. Phoenician script does not show ḥ or ḫ.

Read as “tent” in one Neo-Punic line, “and our tents were opened” (KAI 145 II 10), an interpretation the dictionary itself calls highly problematic. If right, it is a dwelling of a camp, between the verb “encamp” and the chamber חָנוּת.

An Egyptian word borrowed from a Semitic language (the dictionary marks it “Sem. loan word”), the reverse of the usual direction: it shows the Semitic word for spear with ḥ, which Egyptian writes apart from ḫ. It says nothing of how the spear is tied to “bend” or “encamp”.

evidence.locator: tla106190, ḥny.t “spear; javelin (Sem. loan word)” (Wb 3, 110.11; Hoch, Sem. Words, no. 318)

doctrine.statement: The law put outside the camp what could not stay where Yahweh dwelt: the man with the plague of leprosy (Lev 13:46), every unclean person, “that they defile not their camps, in the midst of which I dwell” (Num 5:2–3), and the bodies of the sin offering whose blood was brought into the holy place, burned there with fire (Lev 16:27). The blasphemer and the sabbath-breaker were stoned outside it (Lev 24:14; Num 15:35). When Israel sinned with the calf, Moses pitched the tent outside the camp and everyone who sought Yahweh went out to it (Exo 33:7). Hebrews takes up Lev 16:27: as the bodies of those beasts were burned outside the camp, “Jesus also, that he might sanctify the people with his own blood, suffered outside the gate. Let us go forth therefore to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach” (Heb 13:11–13). From the verses: Christ was put where the law put the sin offering and the unclean, and those who seek him now go out to him, as those who sought Yahweh went out to Moses’ tent.

Israel’s camp was holy because Yahweh was in it: “Yahweh your God walks in the midst of your camp, to deliver you… therefore shall your camp be holy” (Deu 23:15), and the unclean were sent out so as not to defile the camps “in the midst of which I dwell” (Num 5:3). The tribes encamped by their standards around the tent of meeting, with the Levites encamped nearest round the dwelling “that there be no wrath on the congregation” (Num 2:2; 1:53). The camp moved and rested only at Yahweh’s word: “at the mouth of Yahweh they encamped, and at the mouth of Yahweh they set out” (Num 9:18–23), and he went before them “to search out a place for you to encamp” (Deu 1:33). Revelation calls the saints at the end of the thousand years “the camp of the saints, and the beloved city”, compassed by Gog and Magog until fire comes down from God (Rev 20:9). From the verses: God’s people are a camp on the move, kept holy by his presence among them and ordered by his command.

Jacob, met by the angels of God on his way home, said “This is the camp of God” and named the place Mahanaim, “two camps”, beside his own (Gen 32:2–3, 8). “The angel of Yahweh encamps round about those who fear him, and delivers them” (Psa 34:8), and Yahweh says of his house, “I will encamp about my house as a guard” (Zec 9:8). The angel of Yahweh struck the camp of Assyria that encamped against Jerusalem (2Ki 19:35). Hebrews says of the angels, “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for those who shall be heirs of salvation?” (Heb 1:14). From the verses: God’s angels are a host camped about his people for their protection.

note: Drafted 2026-11-13. Root key חנה as the corpus keys it. Left out: the place names מַחֲנֵה־דָן Mahaneh-dan (h.dv.ae; the database’s 32 tokens under that key are all the name Dan, by spelling) and מַחֲנַיִם Mahanaim (h.dv.af), which cannot be name entries; the man תַּחַן Tahan (h.dv.ag; Num 26:35, 1Ch 7:25; TIPNR has two records) and the clan name תַּחֲנִי (h.dv.ah), not given name entries in this task; and the cross-reference keys h.dw.ae, m.bn.bc, w.am.aj, w.am.am, which have no tokens. Gen 32:3 מַחֲנָיִם is counted with the name, its explanation kept under מַחֲנֶה “army” (God’s camp). חַנָּה Hannah and תְּחִנָּה “supplication” belong to חנן, not here. Open questions: (1) How “bend, decline” (Jdg 19:9; Arabic and Syriac ḥny) and “encamp” are one root is not shown by any verse; the summary says so. (2) חֲנִית “spear” has no Semitic cognate sharing its meaning; Egyptian ḥnyt is a loan out of Semitic, which lexicon-support may not count as support. (3) Neh 11:30 and Isa 29:1 (קִרְיַת חָנָה דָוִד) are kept as “encamp”: Neh as settling; Isa 29:1 could be David’s camping against Jebus or his dwelling there, and is not cited. (4) Psa 34:8 is in Hebrew verse numbering (English 34:7). Leads not followed: Payne Smith and Brockelmann for Syriac ḥnā (“bend, incline, aim” per other lexicons) and whether the Peshitta Old Testament uses it for חָנָה; Ge’ez and Old South Arabian not checked (Dillmann, Leslau, Biella); Akkadian ḫanūtu “siege forces” is named by one lexicon but not found in Oracc or checked in CAD, and Akkadian could not show ḥ against ḫ. The Septuagint’s παρεμβάλλω occurs in Luk 19:43 only in critical texts; the Textus Receptus reads περιβαλοῦσιν, so no New Testament verse is given for the verb.
